narrative:
The 2026 New York Mets opened the season with cautious optimism, boasting a lineup anchored by Juan Soto and a rotation headlined by Kodai Senga. But from the very first swing of Opening Day, the warning signs were there — Luis Robert Jr. crushed a three-run homer on March 28 that set the tone for a year in which the Mets would too often find themselves on the wrong end of big moments. The early weeks were a carousel of gut-punch losses and fleeting rallies, a pattern that would define far too much of New York's summer.

The spring months were particularly brutal. Bullpen arms like Devin Williams and Austin Warren became synonymous with late-game disaster, surrendering leads in ways that ranged from heartbreaking to maddening. A grand slam off Huascar Brazobán in late April, CJ Abrams going deep off Luke Weaver, a two-run shot surrendered by Warren in June — the relievers simply could not hold the line. The offense showed flashes, none brighter than Tyrone Taylor's clutch three-run blast on May 17 and Bo Bichette's timely doubles, but the pitching staff's ERA of 4.15 told the story of a team perpetually playing from behind.

July brought the season's most electric individual moment: Juan Soto's three-run homer on July 6 that swung nearly 72 Win Probability points in the Mets' favor — the single biggest play of the year. For a brief stretch, with Luis Torrens delivering a go-ahead double that same day and Devin Williams escaping a jam via double play on July 12, it felt like the Mets might claw their way back into contention. But the wolves kept coming. Senga was lit up for back-to-back home runs in August, and September brought a devastating inside-the-park homer off Jonathan Pintaro that all but slammed the door on any remaining playoff dreams.

In the end, the 2026 Mets finished 74-88, a team whose talent on paper never translated into consistency on the field. A.J. Ewing's three-run shot in the season's final week provided one last moment of pride, a glimpse of what this roster could occasionally be. But 731 runs allowed — more than they scored — and a bullpen that seemed to specialize in catastrophe ensured another October spent watching from home. For the Mets faithful, 2026 was a lesson in how a team can lose a season not in one collapse, but in a hundred small heartbreaks scattered across 162 games.

chapters.title: Stumbling Out of the Gate
chapters.description: The Mets are ambushed on Opening Day and immediately begin fighting an uphill battle through the early weeks of the season.

chapters.title: The Bullpen Catches Fire — The Wrong Kind
chapters.description: A string of late-game meltdowns from the relief corps buries the Mets in the standings as spring turns to early summer.

chapters.title: Soto Sparks a Fleeting Hope
chapters.description: Juan Soto delivers the season's most electrifying moment and a brief cluster of wins revives talk of a comeback.

chapters.title: The Wheels Come Off
chapters.description: August arrives and the rotation crumbles, with Senga battered and the bullpen continuing to bleed runs at every turn.

chapters.title: September Requiem
chapters.description: A devastating inside-the-park homer and a season of accumulated damage seal the Mets' fate, though Ewing offers one last bright note in the final days.
